rounds.proof_sketch: Grid is launched with dim3(outer_size) blocks. CUDA block indices range from 0 to gridDim.x-1, so outer_idx ∈ [0, outer_size-1]. For input shape [128, 4000] with dim=1: outer_size=128, so outer_idx ∈ [0, 127]. Original condition (outer_idx >= 128) is always false. Mutated condition (outer_idx > 128) is also always false. Both conditions never trigger the early return.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the boundary guard from `outer_idx >= outer_size` to `outer_idx > outer_size`. However, this guard is effectively dead code under the current kernel launch configuration. The kernel is launched with exactly `outer_size` blocks via `dim3 grid_size(outer_size)`, meaning `blockIdx.x` (assigned to `outer_idx`) ranges from 0 to `outer_size - 1`. Since `outer_idx` is always strictly less than `outer_size`, both `outer_idx >= outer_size` and `outer_idx > outer_size` evaluate to false for every block. The mutation changes a branch that is never taken, making it semantically equivalent regardless of input tensor values.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable under the fixed-shape contract. The mutation affects a guard condition that never evaluates to true because CUDA block indices are always less than the grid dimension. The difference between >= and > only matters when outer_idx equals outer_size, but this never occurs since blockIdx.x ∈ [0, outer_size-1].
rounds.recommendations: Boundary guard mutations in GPU kernels often become equivalent mutants when the guard protects against conditions that the launch configuration already prevents. To make such guards testable, consider: (1) launching extra blocks intentionally to test guards, (2) using thread-level guards with threadIdx which may have more reachable edge cases, or (3) marking such safety guards as mutation-testing exclusions since they serve as defense-in-depth rather than functional logic.
